about.title: Writing Linear Equations from Information
about.length_note: About 30 minutes. This class has five kinds of starting information (a point and slope, two points, a table, a graph, a story). They all use the same recipe, so one half-hour with a pause after each small step is enough. You can stop after any beat and pick up again later.

sources.title: 4.6 Find the Equation of a Line - Elementary Algebra 2e
High School: Functions (Common Core State Standards for Mathematics)
Find the Equation of a Line (Intermediate Algebra, adapted from OpenStax)
Do two points always determine a linear function?
Do two points always determine a linear function II?

say.text: Today we write the equation of a line from clues: a point and a slope, two points, a table, a graph, or even a story.
First, a reminder. A line can be written y = mx + b. The m is the slope. The b is where the line crosses the y-axis.

ask.why: b is the number added at the end. It is where the line crosses the y-axis. The 3 is the slope.

say.text: If you are told the slope and the y-intercept, you just fill them in. Slope 2 and y-intercept −1 give y = 2x − 1.

show.text: Given: slope m = 2, y-intercept b = −1 | Equation: y = 2x − 1

say.text: Often the point you are given is not on the y-axis. Then we use point-slope form. The point you were given goes in as (x₁, y₁).
Example: slope −2, and the line goes through (3, 1). Put the numbers in the form, and you get y − 1 = −2(x − 3).
Now tidy it into y = mx + b. Multiply out: y − 1 = −2x + 6. Add 1 to both sides: y = −2x + 7.

ask.q: A line has slope 4 and goes through (1, 2). Which equation is it?
ask.why: y − 2 = 4(x − 1) becomes y − 2 = 4x − 4. Add 2 to both sides and you get y = 4x − 2.

say.text: New idea: two points. To use point-slope we need a slope first. Slope is the change in y divided by the change in x.
Example: points (1, 5) and (3, 11). The change in y is 11 − 5 = 6. The change in x is 3 − 1 = 2. So the slope is 6 ÷ 2 = 3.

ask.q: What is the slope between (2, 4) and (6, 12)?
ask.why: The change in y is 12 − 4 = 8. The change in x is 6 − 2 = 4. 8 ÷ 4 = 2.

say.text: One trap. Subtract in the same order on top and on the bottom. If 11 − 5 is on top, then 3 − 1 goes on the bottom, not 1 − 3.

ask.q: Which is a correct slope for the points (2, 3) and (4, 9)?
ask.why: The y's and the x's must be subtracted in the same order. The slope is change in y over change in x, so y goes on top.

say.text: With the slope 3, pick either point. Use (1, 5). Point-slope gives y − 5 = 3(x − 1). Multiply out: y − 5 = 3x − 3. Then add 5.

ask.q: You have y − 5 = 3x − 3. What do you get after adding 5 to both sides?
ask.why: −3 + 5 = 2, so the equation is y = 3x + 2. Adding 5 is the opposite of the −5 on the left.

say.text: Always check with a third point. Our two points built the line, so of course they fit. A new point is a real test. Say (5, 17) is also on the line. Try x = 5: 3 · 5 + 2 = 17. It matches.

ask.q: A friend says (4, 13) is also on y = 3x + 2. Is that right?
wrong: You can't tell without a graph.
ask.why: A point is on the line only if its numbers make the equation true. At x = 4 the line gives y = 14, so (4, 13) is not on it.

say.text: A table is just points in a list. Each row is one point (x, y). Here y goes up by 2 each time x goes up by 1, so the slope is 2. The row with x = 0 shows b = 3.

ask.q: A table has x = 0, 1, 2 and y = 10, 15, 20. What is the equation?
ask.why: y goes up 5 each time x goes up 1, so the slope is 5. When x = 0, y = 10, so b = 10.

say.text: What if there is no x = 0 row? Same idea: use two rows. x goes 2, 4, 6 and y goes 11, 19, 27. From 2 to 4, y rises 8 while x rises 2. That is a slope of 8 ÷ 2 = 4. From 4 to 6 it is the same, so the table is steady.

ask.q: A table has x = 1, 3, 5 and y = 4, 10, 16. What is the slope?
ask.why: From x = 1 to x = 3, y rises 6 while x rises 2. Slope is 6 ÷ 2 = 3.

say.text: Now finish that table. Use the point (2, 11) and slope 4. y − 11 = 4(x − 2). Multiply out: y − 11 = 4x − 8. Add 11: y = 4x + 3. Check with the row (6, 27): 4 · 6 + 3 = 27.

From a graph, pick two points that sit exactly on grid corners, then find the slope. Say the line crosses the y-axis at (0, −1) and passes through (2, 3). The slope is (3 − (−1)) ÷ (2 − 0) = 4 ÷ 2 = 2. So y = 2x − 1.

show.text: A grid with a straight line rising to the right. It crosses the y-axis at (0, −1) and passes through (2, 3). Both points are marked with dots.

ask.q: A line crosses the y-axis at (0, 4) and passes through (1, 1). What is its equation?
ask.why: The slope is (1 − 4) ÷ (1 − 0) = −3. The line crosses the y-axis at 4, so b = 4.

say.text: Stories hide two points too. Sam's game: after 2 hours he has 70 gems, and after 5 hours he has 160. Think of (hours, gems). That gives (2, 70) and (5, 160).
Slope: (160 − 70) ÷ (5 − 2) = 90 ÷ 3 = 30 gems per hour. Use point (2, 70): y − 70 = 30(x − 2). Multiply out: y − 70 = 30x − 60. Add 70: y = 30x + 10.
In a story, the numbers mean something. The 30 is gems earned each hour. The 10 is what you started with. Check with a third fact: at 4 hours Sam had 130, and 30 · 4 + 10 = 130.

show.text: 30 = gems per hour (the rate) | 10 = gems at hour 0 (the start)

ask.q: In y = 30x + 10, what does the 10 mean?
ask.right: The gems Sam had at 0 hours, before he started.
wrong: The gems he earns each hour.
The number of hours to earn 70 gems.
The gems he has after 5 hours.
ask.why: b is the value when x = 0. Here x is hours, so b is the gems at hour 0. The slope, 30, is the gems per hour.

say.text: Here is the whole recipe. It works for every kind of clue, so you only need to learn it once.

show.text: 1. Find the slope (from the words, a table, a graph, or two points). | 2. Put the slope and ONE point into y − y₁ = m(x − x₁). | 3. Tidy it into y = mx + b. | 4. Check with a third point.

say.text: You took a big topic one small step at a time. Next class we look at lines that never meet, and lines that cross at a perfect corner.

notes.topic: Slope formula: change in y over change in x
Point-slope form y − y₁ = m(x − x₁)
Checking an answer by substituting a third point

other_side.claim: With two points, it makes more sense to use point-slope form and then tidy up.
other_side.other_view: OpenStax teaches point-slope for two points. Other teachers, such as Khan Academy, find the slope and then plug one point straight into y = mx + b to solve for b. Both ways give the same line, so use the one that makes more sense to you.

other_side.claim: Two different points always give exactly one line.
other_side.other_view: True, but not every line can be written as y = mx + b. A vertical line can't be written that way because it is not the graph of a function. All lines can still be written as linear equations. Our recipe works for non-vertical lines.
